extracted.intended_audience: news photographers, photo editors, and journalism professionals (photojournalists and contributors)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and ethical criteria for editing, manipulating, captioning, and transmitting news photographs and photo-based images for journalistic use. Covers what edits are permissible, what constitutes manipulation or staging, disclosure and approval procedures, and examples of breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness of AP pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: AP pictures must always tell the truth. We do not alter or digitally manipulate the content of a photograph in any way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute prohibition on altering the factual content of news photographs. Examples of breaches include combining two photos into one (Brian Walski) or removing elements from a frame (Narciso Contreras). AP states reputation is paramount and reacts decisively to violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No elements may be added or subtracted
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of a photograph must not be altered in Photoshop or by any other means. No element should be digitally added to or subtracted from any photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by cases where photographers added smoke, duplicated flares, or removed objects/cameras. Agencies remove manipulated images and may sever ties with photographers who deliberately add/subtract elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not obscure faces or identities
rubrics_metrics.description: The faces or identities of individuals must not be obscured by Photoshop or any other editing tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a source provides an image with obscured identities (e.g., faces hidden), the caption must clearly explain this and transmission must be approved by a senior photo editor. Protecting identity deliberately by editing without disclosure is disallowed for AP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted limited retouching (dust/scratch removal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only retouching or the use of the cloning tool to eliminate dust on camera sensors and scratches on scanned negatives or scanned prints are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the narrow exception to the no-alteration rule. Any other cloning to conceal or alter factual elements (e.g., cloning to hide a photographer's shadow) is unacceptable and has led to removal of images and termination of assignments (Miguel Tovar example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted minor adjustments analogous to darkroom techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor adjustments in Photoshop are acceptable: cropping, dodging and burning, conversion into grayscale, and normal toning and color adjustments limited to those minimally necessary for clear and accurate reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These adjustments should restore or clarify the authentic nature of the photograph, analogous to traditional darkroom burning/dodging. They must be minimal and not change the scene's factual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on substantial changes to density, contrast, color, saturation
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in density, contrast, color and saturation levels that substantially alter the original scene are not acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid aggressive color/contrast edits that create a cinematic or otherworldly look and thus risk misleading viewers about reality. Quoted criticism: such intentions 'alter the reality' and erode public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backgrounds must not be digitally blurred or eliminated
rubrics_metrics.description: Backgrounds should not be digitally blurred or eliminated by burning down or by aggressive toning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altering backgrounds to remove context or create a false emphasis is prohibited because it can misrepresent the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of 'red eye' is not permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: The removal of 'red eye' from photographs is not permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express prohibition in AP's guidance; included as an explicit disallowed edit despite being a common corrective practice elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact senior photo editor with questions/for approval
rubrics_metrics.description: When an employee has questions about the use of such methods or the AP’s requirements and limitations on photo editing, he or she should contact a senior photo editor prior to the transmission of any image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-transmission consultation is required when in doubt; senior editors are the decision point for ambiguous cases to prevent ethical breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and approval for images altered by external sources
rubrics_metrics.description: On those occasions when we transmit images that have been provided and altered by a source — the faces obscured, for example — the caption must clearly explain it. Transmitting such images must be approved by a senior photo editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency in captioning is required whenever an image's content has been altered by others; approval ensures editorial oversight and prevents deceptive use.

rubrics_metrics.name: No staging, posing, or re-enactment for news coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as described herein, we do not stage, pose or re-enact events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When shooting video, environmental portraits, or studio photographs for news, care must be taken not to mislead viewers into believing a posed or re-enacted moment was spontaneously captured. Portraits/fashion/home-design interventions must be revealed in captions and special instructions boxes so they are not mistaken for candid news images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captions must be accurate and not misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: Photograph captions must correctly describe what is depicted and must not mislead viewers about the events or objects shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a photo caption claiming an F-16 was 'firing missiles' was misleading when the plane was dropping flares; such miscaptioning, especially combined with manipulated imagery, leads to retraction and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between enhancement and altering factual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Enhancement to produce a more dramatic image (e.g., adjusting color/contrast for aesthetics) crosses the ethical line when it alters factual elements of the image; the drive to create a more cinematic picture must not lead to changing facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts acceptable aesthetic enhancements with instances where photographers 'went beyond the enhancement into altering the factual elements' (Hajj, Walski). Editors should judge whether edits restore authenticity or modify facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement and consequences for manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations will remove manipulated images from archives, sever ties with contributors, and may fire staff or editors when manipulation or misleading editing is discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple agency examples: LA Times fired Brian Walski for combining photos; Reuters withdrew Adnan Hajj photos and fired a top photo editor; AP severed ties with Narciso Contreras and removed Miguel Tovar's images. Emphasizes zero-tolerance and reputational stakes.
